label: Mercury
catalog_number: Mercury MG-35010 and MGC-109 (10-inch, 1950); first 12-inch compilation Clef MGC-675 (1955)
rationale: Charlie Parker with Strings is the bebop canon's great lyric record: two 1950 Mercury sessions that put Parker's alto in front of a chamber string section and a jazz rhythm section, and the only place in his discography where the ballad side of his playing is the whole argument [S1,S2] (obs). Consensus and institutional standing are documented: the 1955 Clef compilation rates 5/5 at AllMusic and 4/5 in the Penguin Guide, the sessions were Parker's most popular sellers during his lifetime, and they were admitted to the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1988 [S1] (obs). Defining statement: this is the record that answers the question 'what did Parker hear when he heard strings?' — the project he had wanted since at least 1941 ('I asked for strings as far back as 1941', quoted from Priestley in S1), realised under Norman Granz, with Parker's own readings of 'Just Friends', 'April in Paris', 'Summertime' and 'I'll Remember April' as the evidence [S1,S2] (obs). Lineage is unusually direct and unusually well evidenced: S1 states outright that these sessions created a vogue among jazz musicians for recording with strings, naming Clifford Brown with Strings (1955) and Stan Getz's Focus (1961) as the immediate offspring — and Focus is already in the canon, so the influence this record exerted is audible in an album the collection already holds [S1] (obs); the canon's own bebop holdings make the same point from the other side, since the Charlie Parker Story (1945), Bird on 52nd Street (1948) and Bird and Diz (1950) show every Parker idiom except this one (verified against _jazzcanon.album, 2026-11-10) (obs). Session gravity is a different kind than usual for this canon: the rhythm section is Stan Freeman, Ray Brown and Buddy Rich, but the strings and reeds were contracted through Mitch Miller out of the NBC Symphony pool — Frank Brieff, Frank Miller, Milton Lomask — which is exactly the kind of crossover the canon's personnel network exists to record, and three of those players (Milton Lomask, Maurice Brown, Samuel Rand) already appear in the database on Lady in Satin [S1,S2,S3] (obs). It still plays: 'Just Friends' and 'April in Paris' are the standard-bearers, and the July session's 'I'll Remember April' is the one that convinces sceptics [S1,S2] (obs). Scope note for the council: this is an album assembled from two studio sessions and issued first as two 10-inch LPs, later as the 12-inch Clef MGC-675 — the dossier models the 12-track MGC-675 programme and says so in the notes; the remaining two July masters were issued on Mercury MGC-609, and the 1995 Verve Master Takes expands the set with live and 1952 material that is excluded here [S1,S2,S3] (obs).

personnel_record.notes: Two studio sessions, both at Reeves Sound Studios, New York City: November 30, 1949 (producer Norman Granz, arranger/conductor Jimmy Carroll) and July 5, 1950 (arranger/conductor Joe Lipman), per S2 and S1. Release history is genuinely tangled and is recorded rather than smoothed: the 1949 session yielded the six-track 10-inch Mercury MG-35010 (1950); the July 1950 session yielded eight masters issued on the 10-inch Mercury MGC-109 / MGC-509, whose Discogs track order (S3) is Laura, They Can't Take That Away From Me, You Came Along From Out of Nowhere, East of the Sun, Dancing in the Dark, Easy to Love, I'm in the Mood for Love, I'll Remember April. The first 12-inch compilation, Clef MGC-675 (1955), carries twelve of the fourteen masters — six per side — and that is the programme modelled here (S2). The two remaining July masters, 'Dancing in the Dark' (matrix 442-5) and 'Laura' (matrix 444-1), were issued on Mercury MGC-609 Charlie Parker Big Band and are excluded from this track list; the 1995 Verve Charlie Parker with Strings: The Complete Master Takes (24 tracks) adds them back along with five Carnegie Hall titles from September 17, 1950, four January 1952 studio titles and one December 1947 Jazz Scene title, all reissue-era material (S1, S4). Producer: Norman Granz, credited as supervisor and liner-note writer on the Discogs credit block (S3) and named as producer by S1; no recording engineer is named by any source, so engineer is null rather than inferred. Instrument conflicts preserved: Howard Kay is a violin in Wikipedia and Discogs but one of two violas in jazzdisco (recorded violin, unk); Wikipedia lists five violins and one viola for the July session while jazzdisco lists four violins and two violas — Discogs agrees with Wikipedia, so the two-source reading is used and the divergence noted. Name spellings: Caplan/Kaplan, Smirnoff (Zelly/Ziggy), Rosen (Meyer/Myor), Brown (Edwin/Eddie), Mills (Verlye/Verley), Gimpel (Bronislaw/Bronislav), Lipman/Lippman — the majority or database-existing form is used in each case and the variant recorded. The July 1950 dates are also documented as carrying uncredited xylophone and tuba on one title (S1); those players are unnamed in every source consulted, so no personnel row is invented for them. Track personnel arrays follow session membership, not track-level documentation, so every track is marked epistemic inf and track_assignments_complete is false. Apple Music has no edition of this album matching the 12-track 1955 LP; the recorded apple_album_id is the 1995 Complete Master Takes (S4).

ballot.album: Charlie Parker — Charlie Parker with Strings (1950)
ballot.case_for: This is Parker’s defining orchestral statement: bebop’s harmonic and rhythmic intelligence expressed through lyrical standards, with “Just Friends” offering an especially accessible encounter with his improvisational genius. The dossier reports AllMusic’s 5/5, Penguin’s 4/5, Grammy Hall of Fame recognition, and exceptional lifetime popularity, although those claims are mediated through S1 rather than independently supplied reviews. Its strongest lineage argument is the vogue for jazz-with-strings that S1 connects to Clifford Brown with Strings and Stan Getz’s Focus, the latter already represented in this canon. Ray Brown, Buddy Rich, and the orchestral personnel documented in S2–S3 also connect Parker’s experiment to the wider network of canonical orchestral jazz.
ballot.case_against: The string arrangements can sound like conventional commercial sweetening rather than responsive ensemble partners, limiting the rhythmic interaction and collective invention that make small-group bebop compelling. The proposed album artifact also needs precise identification: its twelve-track programme belongs to the 1955 Clef compilation, not a single 1950 release, while the linked digital edition contains substantially more material [S1–S4]. Finally, most evidence for critical consensus and historical influence funnels through Wikipedia; the remaining sources substantiate editions and personnel much more strongly than canonical standing.
ballot.disagreement: Both references judge the album consensus_core and within scope, but differ on urgency: Reference 1 recommends strong, while Reference 2 calls it must_have. They also differ aesthetically over whether the strings provide meaningful counterpoint or largely static accompaniment; the second reference briefly raises an album-artifact boundary but ultimately accepts the compilation, so this is not a substantive scope split.
ballot.recommendation: The council proposes John give this strong-priority consideration as a consensus-core Parker statement, with the twelve-track Clef programme clearly identified and the principal critical claims checked against direct sources.
